corrected_summary: The Utes offered to sell only the existing mines; Brunot declined a mines-only purchase. Ouray's Sept. 13 letter offered mountain land but not valleys. The agreement (Art. II) let the Utes hunt on the ceded land "so long as the game lasts and the Indians are at peace". The cession is about 4 million acres per the 1873 Commissioner report, 3.7 million per 402 U.S. 159, 162; the Royce 566 polygon is 3.8M acres.

corrected_summary: The 1873 agreement reserved any part of Uncompahgre Park lying south of the cession line. Miller's 1875 survey placed it inside the cession. Grant's order of Aug. 17, 1876 withdrew a 4 by 4 mile tract (16 sq. mi.) as part of the reservation. The 1884 Act repealed section 8 of the 1880 Act and restored "the lands referred to in said section" to the public domain; the 1884 Act text does not name Uncompahgre Park.

notes: PSL is internally inconsistent: p.420 calls the survey an "error", p.455 says "deliberately". Neither is established by the EO. On the north line, 330 U.S. 169, 172-173 records that Miller's instructions required a line he admitted was 15 to 18 miles south of the true treaty boundary, which supports a non-accidental survey problem there, not necessarily at the park. Section 8 of the 1880 Act is omitted in Kappler I; confirming that s.8 concerned the park needs 21 Stat. 204 (not in library; only p.199 fetched). Military non-enforcement is PSL only.

source_title: Treaty with the Ute, Mar. 2, 1868, Art. 17 (Kappler II 765-769); 330 U.S. 169
source_quote: Any Indian of either of these confederated bands who shall remain at peace, and abide by the terms of this treaty in all its essentials, shall be entitled to its benefits and provisions
corrected_summary: The Supreme Court itself described the 1880 removal as punishment: "Congress decided to remove the Indians from the Colorado reservation as part of the punishment meted out for this tragedy" (330 U.S. 169, 178). Article 17 of the 1868 treaty preserves benefits for any Ute who stays at peace. That the removal of the peaceful Uncompahgre "contradicts" Art. 17 is PSL's legal argument; formally the 1880 cession was an agreement ratified by Ute signatures, not a forfeiture under Art. 17.
notes: Ouray quote has no citation (PSL says so). Art. 17 actual text reads "may have forfeited", PSL renders "have forfeited".

source_title: ARCIA 1879, Commissioner Hayt report
source_cite: ARCIA 1879, report of the Commissioner, pp. xxxvi-xxxvii

corrected_summary: Hayt's 1879 report did say the Utes held good title to 12 million acres by solemn treaty that "must be lived up to, whether convenient or otherwise". But in the same passage he proposed using that title to buy them out: a commission to obtain their consent "to remove from the State to some other location, say to the Indian Territory", with payment from sale of their Colorado lands.
notes: Do not present the quote as a pro-Ute stance without the removal proposal that follows it.

source_title: ARCIA 1881, Report of the Ute Commission (Uncompahgre removal)
source_cite: 21 Stat. 199-200; ARCIA 1881, Report of the Ute Commission (to Manypenny), pp. ~325-329
source_quote: We examined the land on the Grand River near the mouth of the Gunnison, and found it to be, in our opinion, unsuit- able for the Indians for agricultural or grazing purposes.
corrected_summary: The 1880 agreement sent the Uncompahgre to Grand River near the Gunnison "if a sufficient quantity of agricultural land shall be found there", and otherwise to land "in that vicinity and in the Territory of Utah". The commissioners assigned to the Uncompahgre selection (the report names Mears and Russell building the new agency and McMorris paying improvement claims) reported the Grand River land unsuitable. That this report was knowingly false and motivated by Mears's interest is PSL's accusation, not established by the primary record.
notes: Agreement text confirms the "if a sufficient quantity" condition. The report also says Uncompahgre leaders pressed to stay in the Uncompahgre Valley and were refused. Grand Junction area was opened to settlement soon after (not checked here).

source_title: Act of June 15, 1880, ch. 223 (Kappler I 181-182)
source_quote: The Southern Utes agree to remove to and settle upon the unoccu¬ pied agricultural lands on the La Plata River, in Colorado
corrected_summary: Agreement text confirmed. Royce (p.899) records that insufficient agricultural land was found and the Southern Utes stayed on the strip they occupied (Royce 617). Manypenny's two surveys are PSL only.
notes: Royce 616 is the ceded north/central tract; the La Plata provision concerns the Southern Ute strip, 617.

source_title: ARCIA 1881, Report of the Ute Commission, Jan. 20, 1881 (signed Manypenny, Meacham, Bowman, Russell, Mears)
source_cite: ARCIA 1881, Report of Ute Commission pp.201-207; 21 Stat. 199-200 (three-fourths proviso)
source_quote: It was found that the names obtained at both agencies aggregated 581 adult male Ute Indians of the confederated bands in Colorado.
corrected_summary: The 1880 Act required signatures of three-fourths of adult males. The Ute Commission reported 581 adult male signatures by Sept. 25, 1880, which it judged over three-fourths, and noted Ouray's death and Kaniache's death by lightning. Its report, signed by chairman Manypenny and by Mears, says signers acted "without restraint and of their own accord", and records that Southern Ute signers expected "the money promised them" (the $60,000 per capita distribution provided in the agreement). The $2 per signature payments by Mears, Manypenny's refusal to approve, and Kirkwood's reimbursement come from Conetah (1982) via PSL and are not supported by this record; Manypenny signed the report that treated ratification as complete.
notes: Contradiction on Manypenny "would not approve the agreement". Keep $2 claim as attributed (Conetah) only. Ouray non-signature: report shows Ouray said on July 26 no Uncompahgre was ready to sign; his own signature not checked.

source_title: ARCIA 1881, Uintah/Uncompahgre agent report (Berry) on removal
source_quote: This lefusal to comply with my request resulted in their being turned over by the department to the charge of General R. S. Mackenzie
corrected_summary: The agent's 1881 report confirms the Uncompahgre refused to go, were placed under General Mackenzie's military control, then agreed to move; rations were issued Aug. 27, 1881 and they departed. The 24-hour ultimatum, artillery, 1,400 people and 350 miles are from Conetah and other sources via PSL. The agent describes the departure as "apparently cheerful", which should be read as a self-serving official account. Mears building the road and agency is supported: the commission report says Mears and Russell went to erect the new agency buildings.
notes: Row quote "24 hours to prepare" spans a line in PSL (string matches with whitespace). Military coercion is primary-confirmed.

source_title: United States v. Southern Ute Tribe or Band of Indians, 402 U.S. 159 (1971)
source_quote: We therefore hold that the claim in this case is res judicata under the 1950 consent judgment enforcing the settlement agreement
corrected_summary: The ICC rejected the Government's res judicata defense in 1966 (17 Ind. Cl. Comm. 28) and again on remand in 1969 (21 Ind. Cl. Comm. 268); the Court of Claims affirmed (423 F.2d 346). The Supreme Court reversed (Douglas dissenting), holding that the plain wording of the 1880 Act ceded all nonallotted land including the Southern Ute strip (Royce 617), so the 1950 consent judgment (Case No. 46640, 117 Ct. Cl. 433) barred the claim. The attorney in the 1950 stipulation is called "Dr. Wilkinson"; Ernest L. Wilkinson and Glen A. Wilkinson represented the Utes in this era. Charles Wilkinson is wrong.
notes: The claim as filed covered about 220,000 acres disposed of as free homesteads and 82,000 acres unaccounted (402 U.S. at 159-160); 230,547.44 and 81,953.18 are PSL figures from ICC findings, not checked. July 14, 1971 date not checked. Ernest L. Wilkinson argued 330 U.S. 169 for the Utes; Glen A. Wilkinson argued 402 U.S. 159.

source_quote: the aboriginal title of the Western Shoshone had been extinguished in the latter part of the 19th century
corrected_summary: The ICC (1962) held Western Shoshone aboriginal title extinguished in the latter part of the 19th century and later (1977) awarded over $26 million; the Court of Claims affirmed in 1979. The "gradual encroachment by whites" wording, the July 1, 1872 valuation date and the 24.4M acre figure are from the ICC opinion, which was not reachable.
notes: Settle exact wording with 11 Ind. Cl. Comm. 387.

source_title: United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, 448 U.S. 371 (1980); Act of Feb. 28, 1877
source_quote: the court held that the Sioux were entitled to an award of interest on the principal sum of $17.1 million (the fair market value of the Black Hills as of 1877), dating from 1877
notes: "A more ripe and rank case of dishonorable dealings will never, in all probability, be found in our history" is in the opinion, quoting the Court of Claims; it is now confirmed. Interest rate 5%. The $106M figure and fund size are secondary. Polygons recomputed: 597 21.3M, 598 7.2M (598 typed "statute").

source_title: City of Sherrill v. Oneida Indian Nation, 544 U.S. 197 (2005); County of Oneida v. Oneida Indian Nation, 470 U.S. 226 (1985)
source_quote: evoke the doctrines of laches, acquiescence, and impossibility, and render inequitable the piecemeal shift in governance this suit seeks unilaterally to initiate
corrected_summary: Oneida II (1985) held the Oneidas had a federal common-law action for violation of possessory rights; the claim concerned New York's 1795 purchase, not the 1788 Fort Schuyler treaty. Sherrill (2005) barred the Nation from reviving sovereignty over parcels it repurchased, on laches, acquiescence and impossibility.

source_title: Joint Resolution for annexing Texas, Mar. 1, 1845, as quoted in Texas Ordinance of July 4, 1845; atlas grid
source_quote: shall also retain all the vacant and unappropriated lands lying within its limits
corrected_summary: Texas kept its public lands at annexation (5 Stat. 797). Five Royce polygons touch Texas (478, 511, 512, 513, 688). The central Texas box (94-103W, 28-33N) is about 45% covered on the repo grid, but mostly by Royce 478 (Kiowa-Comanche, about 41% of the box), not Apache 688 (about 11%). The 1854 twelve-league reserves and 1859 removal were not checked against Texas statutes.
notes: Avalon page is the Texas ordinance quoting the resolution; library 5 Stat. 797 file has only the first page.

source_title: Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, Pub. L. 92-203; Tee-Hit-Ton Indians v. United States, 348 U.S. 272 (1955)
source_quote: including any aboriginal hunting or fishing rights that may exist, are hereby extinguished
corrected_summary: ANCSA extinguished all aboriginal title and claims in Alaska. Its fund was $462.5M from the Treasury plus $500M in revenue sharing ($962.5M). Land grants in the Act text are about 40M acres (22M village, 16M regional remainder of 38M, 2M other); 44-45M is a later conveyance figure. Tee-Hit-Ton held "the taking by the United States of unrecognized Indian title is not compensable under the Fifth Amendment".

source_title: Apology Resolution, Pub. L. 103-150; Newlands Resolution
source_quote: never directly relinquished their claims to their inherent sovereignty as a people or over their national lands to the United States
notes: This is a "Whereas" recital, not an operative finding; the Resolution also recites the 1.8M-acre cession "without the consent of or compensation to the Native Hawaiian people". Hawaii v. OHA, 556 U.S. 163 (2009) held it created no substantive rights (not re-checked).

source_title: Mountain States Tel. & Tel. Co. v. Pueblo of Santa Ana, 472 U.S. 237 (1985), quoting S. Rep. No. 492, 68th Cong. 1st Sess. (1924)
source_quote: there are now approximately 3,000 claimants to lands within the exterior boundaries of the Pueblo grants. The non-Indian claimants with their families comprise about 12,000 per- sons
corrected_summary: The 3,000 claimants / 12,000 persons figures are confirmed (S. Rep. 492 quoted in 472 U.S. 237). The phrase "moral, if not legal, obligation to make reasonable restitution" does not appear in 472 U.S. 237; its source is unverified.
notes: Pueblo grants were confirmed by Act of Dec. 22, 1858 (11 Stat. 374), per Royce p.922.
